nameStory: The 'flying' in flying squirrel is a bit misleading — these acrobatic mammals don't actually fly like birds or bats! Instead, they glide gracefully through the forest canopy using a furry membrane stretched between their front and back legs, like a living parachute. The 'southern' part of their name distinguishes them from their northern cousins who prefer cooler climates.
description: Southern flying squirrels are small, soft-furred mammals about the size of a hamster, with big dark eyes perfect for their nighttime lifestyle. Their most remarkable feature is the stretchy skin flap called a patagium that connects their front and back legs, allowing them to glide up to 80 feet between trees. Their silky gray-brown fur and flat, feathery tail help them navigate their aerial highways through New England's forests. Adults typically measure 8-10 inches long with an equally long tail.

idTips.label: Gliding Membrane
idTips.description: The furry patagium stretches from wrist to ankle on each side, visible as loose skin folds when the squirrel is at rest. When spread, it creates a perfect square gliding surface that feels like soft velvet.

idTips.label: Size & Shape
idTips.description: Much smaller than tree squirrels — about the size of a hamster with a flattened body profile. Large, bulging black eyes dominate their small face, giving them an almost cartoon-like appearance.

idTips.label: Fur
idTips.description: Incredibly soft, dense fur that's gray-brown on top and creamy white underneath. The texture is silkier than any tree squirrel — almost like touching a rabbit's belly.

idTips.label: Tail
idTips.description: Flattened horizontally like a feather rather than bushy and round. Acts as a rudder during glides and feels much flatter and softer than a gray squirrel's tail.

idTips.label: Behavior
idTips.description: Strictly nocturnal — you'll never see them during daylight hours. Listen for soft chittering calls and gentle thumps as they land on tree trunks after gliding.

idTips.label: Sign
idTips.description: Look for small, round holes in dead trees where they nest, and tiny gnaw marks on nuts and acorns. Their droppings are smaller than other squirrels — about the size of rice grains.

habitat: Southern flying squirrels prefer mature deciduous and mixed forests with plenty of old trees for nesting cavities. They're especially common in oak-hickory forests where they can find abundant nuts, and areas with dense canopy cover that provides good gliding routes. You'll find them from lowland forests up to mid-elevation mountains throughout New England.

seasonality.spring: Active at night feeding on tree buds, flowers, and emerging insects. This is breeding season, so listen for increased chattering and activity in the canopy.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period with young squirrels learning to glide. They're busy collecting insects, bird eggs, and early fruits during warm nights.
seasonality.fall: Frantically gathering and caching nuts and acorns for winter storage. They may share communal nests and are most vocal during this preparation time.
seasonality.winter: Less active but don't hibernate — they huddle together in tree cavities for warmth. On warmer winter nights, they emerge to feed on stored nuts and tree bark.

funFact: Flying squirrels are among the only mammals that glow bright pink under ultraviolet light! Scientists discovered this accidentally and still don't fully understand why their belly fur fluoresces like a blacklight poster.
confusionNotes: Most often confused with regular tree squirrels seen at dusk, but flying squirrels are strictly nocturnal and much smaller. If you see a 'squirrel' gliding between trees or active after full dark, it's definitely a flying squirrel — tree squirrels can't glide and are rarely active at night.
contextualKnowledge: Despite their name, flying squirrels are more closely related to chipmunks than to tree squirrels. Many people live their entire lives in flying squirrel habitat without ever seeing one due to their nocturnal nature, even though they can be quite common.
compareHints: Southern flying squirrels are smaller and grayer than their northern flying squirrel relatives, with less contrast between their back and belly colors. Northern flying squirrels prefer coniferous forests and have slightly larger eyes and more cinnamon-colored fur. In areas where both species overlap, southerns stick to deciduous trees while northerns prefer evergreens.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Northern flying squirrels are significantly larger than southern flying squirrels and prefer cooler, higher elevation coniferous forests rather than the mixed hardwood forests favored by their southern relatives.
